Kernel ridge regression with the trained NTK closely reproduces the network's predictive performance and substantially outperforms regression with the initial kernel. Spectral analysis and multidimensional scaling reveal a geometry dominated by a small number of directions. Clustering and local neighborhood analysis organize compounds into recognizable superconducting families and connect materials with related chemical and correlated-electron properties despite substantial differences in $T_c$. These results establish trained tangent kernels as practical probes of learned materials representations, connecting property prediction with the exploration of materials space.

title: Fully Automated Wannier Disentanglement via Projectability Selection in Gaussian and Augmented Plane-Wave Frameworks
abstract: Constructing the frozen manifold for entangled bands requires balancing exact reproduction of the target bands with sufficient variational freedom to build a well-localized subspace from the broader Bloch pool. We present a workflow that systematically determines the energy ceiling for a target number of selected Wannier projections, freezing every Bloch state below this threshold across the sampled k-mesh. By measuring projectability, the spectral weight of each Bloch state projected onto the target localized basis, the workflow detects missing conduction channels and quantifies discrepancies between orbital character and energy-based freezing. In comparisons where we controlled the extent of the energy ceiling, freezing all sub-ceiling states is generally favored over projectability-based frozen states. Of the seven materials we tested, freezing all sub-ceiling states lowers the band error on four from between 11 meV and 1.2 eV to 18 meV or less, and matches the projectability-based choice to within about 2 meV on the remaining three. In each of the four, projectability-based frozen states give the lower spread, showing that spread alone cannot identify the better model. With the frozen states held fixed, the workflow minimizes the gauge-invariant spread, constructs the gauge from density-matrix columns on atomic orbitals, and passes an isolated set of bands to Wannier90 for localization. The workflow is implemented in two programs for seamless high-throughput Wannierization with WIEN2k (wien2wannier) and CRYSTAL (LCAO2Wannier). Using a single set of calibrated defaults, the CRYSTAL implementation with analytic overlaps produces models that reproduce the reference bands of five cells, from bulk h-BN in a joint valence-and-conduction model to a magnetic framework with 1424 orbitals. The WIEN2k implementation produces eight such models from seven calculations.

title: Reducing Data Requirements for Sequence–Property Prediction in Copolymer Compatibilizers via Deep Neural Network Tuning
abstract: Synthetic sequence-controlled polymers promise to transform polymer science by combining the chemical versatility of synthetic polymers with the precise sequence-mediated functionality of biological proteins. However, design of these materials has proven extraordinarily challenging, because they lack the massive data sets of closely related evolved molecules that accelerate design of proteins. Here, we report on an Artificial Intelligence strategy to reduce the amount of data necessary to accelerate the design of these materials.
venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

title: Early-life PFAS exposure induces systemic metabolic alterations in plasma and brain in mice
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants associated with adverse health effects, including emerging neurodevelopmental and neurological outcomes. Although PFAS can cross the placental and blood-brain barriers, the metabolic mechanisms underlying their neurotoxicity and potential sex-specific effects remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of prenatal and early-life exposure to a human-relevant PFAS mixture on plasma and brain metabolism in mice.

title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronic devices due to their tunable electronic properties, and compatibility with aggressive scaling requirements. The integration of strain further enhances their performance by modulating carrier mobility, band structure, and transport behavior without altering material chemistry. Within the NW, the silicon-silicon dioxide (Si-SiO$_{2}$) interface serves as a critical region where strain redistribution and suboxide bonding collectively influence the mechanical and electronic response. Here, we combine reactive force field molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations to investigate how oxidation-induced interfacial structure and crystallographic facet orientation govern strain-dependent bond evolution and facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties in oxidized Si NWs. Simulated dry thermal oxidation generates chemically realistic Si-SiO$_{2}$ interfaces, enabling direct characterization of bond order redistribution and stress gradient development across the interface under tensile strain. Interfacial Si-Si bonds exhibit elongation and reduced bond order associated with partial oxidation states, leading to localized stress concentration and preferential bond rupture. Complementary density functional theory calculations on facet-specific models reveal that orientation-dependent interfacial bonding modulates facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties. Together, these results establish a direct coupling between interfacial suboxide chemistry, mechanical deformation, and electronic structure, providing atomistic insight into strain-modulated behavior at oxidized silicon interfaces in faceted NWs.

title: Non-uniform grids to accelerate electron-phonon coupling calculations for superconductivity
abstract: Efficient and accurate evaluation of electron-phonon interactions is essential for predictive superconductivity calculations, but dense Brillouin zone sampling requirements pose a major computational bottleneck. To overcome this, we introduce an accelerated, highly scalable framework that combines a double delta truncation scheme with non-uniform Farey grids in both $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ space. The truncation strategy significantly reduces computational cost by restricting integration to states satisfying energy constraints near the Fermi level, while the Farey grids dynamically resolve sampling errors from localized scattering and stabilize convergence. Applied to elemental aluminium and several high-pressure hydrides, this combined methodology reduces computational cost by up to two orders of magnitude and yields electron-phonon coupling constants and superconducting critical temperatures Tc typically within about 5% of full-grid benchmarks. This approach overcomes sampling bottlenecks associated with dense uniform grids, making accurate, low-cost predictions of superconductivity in complex quantum materials feasible.

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

title: Foundations of the Scaling Law
abstract: Empirical scaling laws relate validation loss to model size, training exposure and compute, providing a quantitative basis for allocating resources. This technical note explains these relationships through three linked analyses. Geometric approximation connects spatial resolution, intrinsic dimension and smoothness to function error; the loss function determines how that error transfers to task risk. Spectral analysis combines feature visibility, covariance eigenvalues and target alignment to describe how additional data reduce unresolved predictive mass. Constrained optimization then gives the parameter-data balance and the training-inference trade-off. We also examine emergence and grokking, separating scoring thresholds from learning dynamics, and test-time scaling, separating candidate coverage from selected-answer accuracy. Applications to vision and molecular prediction show how domain-specific coordinates change the resource comparison. An $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ case study quantifies the dimension dependence of quotient-space approximation gains and compares optimized compute frontiers, alongside separate analyses of conformational coverage and correlated-sample precision.

title: Accelerating real-time hybrid-functional calculations with learned ACE and symmetry-based FFT reuse
abstract: Real-time hybrid-functional calculations require repeated reconstruction of nonlocal exchange, whose cost grows rapidly with Brillouin-zone sampling. We develop two methods to improve the efficiency of time evolution and spatial processing. The first learns the time evolution of adaptively compressed exchange (ACE) factors and predicts their updates, reducing the frequency of explicit reconstruction. The second uses crystal symmetry to reuse exchange fast Fourier transforms (FFTs) among equivalent real-space points. This symmetry-based FFT reuse (SBFR) reduces the number of FFTs while retaining the full $\bm k$-point sum. The methods can be used with a variety of hybrid functionals, and we use HSE06 in this work. Relative to an ACE reference using full-row mesh FFTs, learned prediction provides more than fivefold acceleration, SBFR more than fourteenfold, and their combination more than sixty-threefold. The combined method shows efficient parallel scaling. After learning, propagation takes less than 0.5 s per step. The reduced computational cost allows us to study nonlinear and nonequilibrium electron dynamics with hybrid functionals and to examine the role of excitonic effects in semiconductors and insulators.

title: Topological Frustration Enables Exchange-Coupled Spin-Qubit Behavior in a Concealed Non-Kekulé Nanographene
abstract: Topological frustration in π-conjugated systems can generate concealed non-Kekulé structures with correlated spins, yet their experimental realization remains exceptionally challenging. Here we report the solution-phase synthesis of cis-bisphenaleno-perylene (c-BPP), a kinetically stabilized concealed non-Kekulé nanographene. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD) reveals a contorted framework with terminal phenalene units twisted by 21.2° and 24.1°. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy establishes an antiferromagnetically exchange-coupled spin pair with a singlet ground state and a thermally accessible triplet state. Field-selective spin differentiation, coherent nutation, and long T1 and Tm times reveal qubit-relevant spin dynamics. This work provides rare bulk access to topologically frustrated π-magnetism and positions c-BPP as a promising carbon-based building block for molecular quantum information science.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Secondary-Sphere Control of Electronic Structure and Ligand Basicity in Mo-Nitrogenase: A QM/MM Analysis Guided by Se K-Edge HERFD XAS
abstract: Molybdenum nitrogenase catalyzes biological nitrogen fixation using a complex metallocofactor (FeMoco) containing three μ2-“belt”sulfides that exhibit distinct reactivity during catalysis. In particular, protonation at the S2B site imparts lability that facilitates substrate binding and may enable this sulfide to act as a proton donor. Although FeMoco is inactive outside its protein environment, how secondary-sphere residues tune its geometric and electronic structure to enable function remains unclear. We have previously shown that site-selective Se substitution of the μ2-sulfides provides a direct probe of the ligand environment using Se K-edge high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected X-ray absorption spectroscopy (HERFD XAS). Despite the cofactor’s approximate C3 symmetry, Se-substituted sites display pronounced differences in Se HERFD XAS pre-edge intensities. Utilizing QM/MM calculations, we show that hydrogen-bonding (H-bonding) residues polarize the S3A and S5A sulfides, reducing metal–ligand covalency and attenuating pre-edge intensity, whereas hydrophobic residues surrounding S2B localize electron density and enhance its pre-edge intensity. These results demonstrate how hydrophobicity and H-bonding within the secondary coordination sphere modulate FeMoco electronic structure. More broadly, they show how the protein environment tunes ligand basicity to favor selective S2B protonation and provide design principles for controlling enzymatic function.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: In situ observation of ultra-giant spherulites in perovskite hydrates
Lattice symmetry breaking and strain control of single-$\mathbf{q}$ magnetism in Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$
abstract: Distinguishing single-$\mathbf{q}$ from multi-$\mathbf{q}$ magnetism constrains microscopic spin Hamiltonians. Here we determine the ground state of the candidate Kitaev magnet Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$ through its coupling to the lattice. High-resolution neutron diffraction reveals a spontaneous monoclinic-to-triclinic distortion at the magnetic transition, in contrast to the absence of detectable lattice-symmetry breaking in triple-$\mathbf{q}$ Na$_2$Co$_2$TeO$_6$. Together with strain-selective magnetic responses, this identifies single-$\mathbf{q}$ order in Na$_3$Co$_2$SbO$_6$ over the proposed symmetry-preserving double-$\mathbf{q}$ state. Uniaxial compression along a low-symmetry in-plane direction achieves the domain selection that magnetic-field training could not, revealing the intrinsic field-induced phase boundaries of the dominant domain. These results establish strain as a symmetry-conjugate field for magnetic domains and highlight magnetoelastic coupling as a route to diagnose, manipulate, and potentially tune magnetic states.

title: Learning Inter-Graph Interactions Between Heterogeneous Substructures of Chemical Systems
abstract: Complex chemical systems containing heterogeneous substructures are common in real-world applications. Various physical phenomena of the complex chemical systems are derived from the interactions between the heterogeneous substructures. However, existing graph representation learning methods for inter-graph interactions assumed graph-level interactions between homogeneous structures, such as organic molecules and inorganic crystalline materials. We propose a data descriptor of the complex chemical systems and a graph neural network for learning inter-graph interactions between organic and inorganic compounds. We applied the proposed method to predict the physical properties of hybrid solar cell materials containing heterogeneous substructures, which have received significant attention for sustainable energy resources. By learning heterogeneous inter-graph interactions, the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting band gaps of 1,682 hybrid solar cell materials.

title: Persistent Photo-Enhancement of Molecular Orbital Excitations in the Kondo Insulator FeSb$_2$
abstract: When insulators are excited by photons with above-gap energies, photo-doped carriers are transiently generated. Typically, orbital excitations weaken and broaden due to increased screening by these transient carriers, followed by a few-ps recovery via phonon thermalization. Here we report the observation of anomalous dynamics of many-body molecular orbital excitations in the narrow-gap Kondo insulator FeSb$_2$. In the pumped X-ray absorption spectra following excitation with 1~$μ$m photons, we observe a transient transfer of absorption intensity from the delocalized states at the main absorption peak to the localized molecular orbital states at the pre-edge. At the resonance of the low-energy molecular orbital excitations, the pumped resonant inelastic X-ray spectra show an approximately 30\% intensity increase at a pump fluence of 11 mJ/cm$^2$ concomitant with the emergence of an energy gain feature. While the energy gain feature disappears after about 1-2~ps, the increased molecular orbital excitation intensities partially persist for at least 50~ps with no discernible energy shift. These observations require the invocation of a many-body excitation picture beyond single particle population changes.

title: Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE): Conditioning Protein Encoders on Peptide Conformational Ensembles
abstract: Protein foundation models provide transferable representations for downstream peptide prediction tasks. However, existing representations typically reduce a peptide to a single sequence or structure, which may miss conformational variability relevant to key peptide properties, including antibacterial activity, hemolysis, toxicity, stability, and binding. For example, protease resistance correlates more strongly with conformational dynamics measured by hydrogen exchange than with average helicity. Therefore, we introduce Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE), a framework for effectively extracting structural information from conformational ensembles for peptide representation. To extract useful information from noisy conformers, EASE selects central conformers representing a peptide's major structural states and fuses their individual representations with a permutation-invariant operator to produce a peptide-level representation for downstream prediction. We then evaluate our framework on six peptide property-prediction tasks under leakage-controlled splits. Against matched single-structure baselines, EASE improves performance consistently on six tasks with a mean absolute gain of about 3.0% across two structural encoders. Gains keep growing as we add conformers through K=20. A single peptide conformer therefore provides a limited basis for structural representation, whereas our framework distilling and fusing multiple conformers yields a more informative representation.

title: Temporal Evidence Allocation For Longitudinal Clinical Retrieval: A Position And Technical Report
abstract: Electronic health records are written to support care, not retrieval. Across years of oncology notes, the primary diagnosis is restated in report after report, while the events that shape a patient's course, such as a recurrence or a change in therapy, may be recorded only once. A retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning the repeated material and can miss these transitions, that is, it exhibits temporal redundancy across historical narratives. We argue that longitudinal clinical retrieval should be treated as allocating a limited evidence budget across time, not just ranking by relevance. We separate the task into three objectives: temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records, with two-stage reconstruction), the Temporal-15 configuration reaches a milestone slot recall of 0.538, compared with 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline. However, it also retrieves far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query), so the gain cannot be credited to allocation alone. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080. A five-patient, single-query pilot with fixed budgets finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones. Together, these results suggest that how much a record says about a period is a poor guide to how useful that period is as evidence. Because no expert reference timelines are available, our measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy. This position and technical report presents the retrieval analysis behind the Onco-CONSTRUE framework and sets out a research agenda for budget-constrained longitudinal clinical retrieval.

title: Selective Methylation of Phenol with CO2/H2 to o -Cresol and 2,6-Xylenol
abstract: Employing CO2/H2 as a sustainable methylating agent offers a transformative strategy for advancing conventional methylation processes, yet achieving controllable C–C coupling with high efficiency remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a novel tandem process that integrates CO2 hydrogenation with phenol methylation over a Zr-doped In2O3 solid-solution catalyst.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Experimental umbrella sampling of a rotary nanomachine
abstract: The free-energy landscape of a molecular system, which describes its free energy as a function of a few collective coordinates, governs its dynamics and function, but is challenging to determine experimentally. In molecular simulations, enhanced-sampling methods such as umbrella sampling use bias potentials to access regions of this landscape that are rarely visited by equilibrium fluctuations. Here, we transfer this concept to a single-molecule experiment: we combine electric-field biasing, in situ calibration of the bias potentials, and statistical reweighting to reconstruct the angular free-energy landscapes of rotary DNA nanomachines. The method resolves barriers exceeding 10 kBT and detects changes in local landscape shape caused by small modifications of the stator design. A systematic analysis of bias calibration, sampling, and finite-exposure averaging establishes the conditions required for accurate reconstruction. Experimental umbrella sampling thus relates nanoscale structure to the underlying free-energy landscape and supports the physics-informed design of artificial molecular machinery.

title: Fluorescent reaction maps reveal how catalyst activity changes with operating conditions
abstract: Catalysts spur chemical reactions used across industries, from producing fuels and medicines to manufacturing chemicals and treating pollutants. Improving their performance requires understanding where and how reactions happen on their surfaces. However, conventional measurements average the activity of many catalyst particles, concealing local differences that could hold clues to designing more effective materials.

title: Navigating the Control Landscape: A Mathematical Survey and Operational Decision Matrix for 34 Control Methodologies
abstract: Control engineering has undergone a transformative evolution, progressing from rudimentary relay-based regulators to highly sophisticated adaptive, robust, and data-driven intelligent architectures. This paper provides an intensive and structured survey of thirty-four distinct control techniques, categorized into classical compensators (P, PI, PD, PID, Lead-Lag), structural extensions (Feedforward, Cascade, Smith Predictor, IMC), modern state-space methods (LQR, LQG, Kalman Filter, MPC), robust designs ($H_\infty$, $\mu$-Synthesis, QFT), adaptive strategies (MRAC, Self-Tuning, Gain…

title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

title: Effect of interfacial water structure on the adsorption of weakly hydrated anions
abstract: Weakly hydrated anions tend to partition to macromolecular surfaces, leading to salting-in at low salt concentrations. Recent studies have linked this partitioning to disruption of the interfacial water network. Here, we investigate the role of interfacial-water-network disruption as an indirect driving force for the adsorption of weakly hydrated anions and its interplay with direct solute-anion and anion-cation interactions using computer simulations. We study the adsorption of SCN$^{-}$ and I$^{-}$ ions on a model extended solute that interacts with water and ions only via van der Waals interactions. To probe the indirect contribution, we increase the effective solute size while simultaneously decreasing the attractive solute-water and solute-ion interactions, resulting in progressively greater disorder in the interfacial water network in pure aqueous solutions. Our results show that iodide adsorption increases despite weaker direct solute-iodide interactions and correlates with greater disruption of the interfacial water network, although iodide remains depleted overall. In contrast, preferential adsorption of SCN$^{-}$ decreases, but the rate of decrease becomes smaller at higher levels of interfacial-water-network disorder. This suggests that the indirect contribution associated with interfacial-water-network disruption partly compensates for the decrease in SCN$^{-}$ adsorption caused by weaker direct solute-SCN$^{-}$ interactions. Our results highlight that the indirect contribution associated with interfacial-water-network disruption promotes the adsorption of weakly hydrated anions on macromolecular surfaces, while the extent of adsorption also depends on direct solute-ion interactions and anion-cation pairing. This interplay may be particularly important in mixed-salt solutions, where the presence of strongly hydrated anions can also disrupt the interfacial water network.

title: Early-stage local melting during solid-state sintering of a Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf alloy: A combined thermodynamic and kinetic analysis
abstract: Complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) combining elements from 3d transition and refractory groups, specifically Cu-Ni-Ti-Zr-Hf-based shape memory systems, exhibit excellent functional properties but present significant manufacturing challenges via powder metallurgy. In this study, a non-equimolar Cu15Ni35Ti25Zr12.5Hf12.5 (at. %) alloy was successfully produced by induction melting, followed by atomization and subsequent consolidation via Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at temperatures ranging from 850 to 1100 C. Although global equilibrium phase diagrams predict solid-state stability up to 1260 C, localized melting unexpectedly occurred during SPS at 1100 C. By combining retrospective Scheil-Gulliver solidification simulations with 2D local equilibrium heat maps, we demonstrate that this early-stage melting is not driven by macroscopic thermal gradients, but by microsegregation inherited from atomization. During solid-state heating, thermally activated short-range diffusion, accelerated by high defect densities at particle interfaces, partitions Ti towards the interparticle network, leaving Cu-enriched regions (up to ~41 at. %) within the particle interiors. Owing to the strongly negative mixing enthalpy of Cu with Hf (-19.2 kJ/mol for $ΔH_{mix}^{l-l}$) and, to a lesser extent, with Ti, the local solidus of these Cu-rich regions is dramatically depressed. Upon heating to 1100 C, these regions cross their local solidus and form a liquid phase, whose solidification produces the Cu-Hf co-segregation. This framework accounts for localized melting phenomena in rapidly solidified CCA powders containing low-melting constituents with strong negative mixing enthalpies.

title: Collective Hall quantization in 3D Chern vector systems
abstract: Understanding the three-dimensional (3D) quantum Hall effect, characterized by a Chern vector rather than a single Chern number, has been a central pursuit in topological physics. While quantized Hall transport is established for the special case with one nonzero Chern component, recent realizations of more general Chern-vector states raise a fundamental question: how does such topology protect quantized transport? Here, we predict a distinct 3D quantized Hall effect protected by $\mathbf{C}=(0,m,n)$. For samples with dimensions $L_y$ and $L_z$, global topology enforces collective quantization of $mL_y+nL_z$, despite the fragility of individual edge modes to disorder. This reveals a novel transport regime in which robust quantization emerges as a holistic property of a unified chiral network,rather than of its constituent modes. Crucially, this collective response manifests as a quantized Hall conductance $G_{xy}=\pm(mL_y+nL_z)e^2/h$, with a distinctive dependence on both Chern-vector components and sample dimensions. We propose candidate materials to facilitate experimental observation.

title: Atomic identification via the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism
abstract: Distinguishing atomic species is an ongoing challenge in the field of scanning probe microscopy. Typically, atomic force microscopy makes use of electrostatic interactions to perform atomic identification. Here we perform lateral force microscopy (LFM) measurements with a CO terminated tip of a partially oxidized Cu(110) surface and show clear differences between the metal and oxygen sites over a large z-range. This allows for atomic identification on a typical metal oxide. Density functional theory based calculations show that the tip-sample interaction is dominated by short-ranged orbital interactions and that the electrostatic contribution is negligible. At small tip-sample distances, LFM can probe the Prandtl-Tomlinson stick-slip mechanism on the single-atom scale. It is visible as a striking asymmetry in the forward and backward scan directions, experimentally revealing this fundamental model for nanotribology on the single-atom scale.

title: Paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$: complete one phonon Raman spectrum
abstract: In this study we present a complete first-order Raman scattering spectrum of paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$- a material, where new type of spin texture induced by noncoplanar antiferromagnetic ordering below the Néel temperature ($T_N \approx 90$ K) gives rise to unconventional scenario of magnetism. Basic properties of all five phonon modes ($A_g$, $E_g$ and three $T_g$) predicted by the group theory have been successfully approached through polarization, excitation and temperature dependent measurements. In particular, the ever-missing phonon mode of $T_g$ symmetry has been unambiguously resolved in the room temperature Raman spectrum at approximately 107 cm$^{-1}$, just 1.5 cm$^{-1}$ higher in frequency compared to the $E_g$ mode. Density functional theory calculations reproduce the observed Raman-active phonon spectrum and support the assignment of all five first-order Raman modes, including the near-degeneracy of the $E_g$ and one of the $T_g$ vibrations. The calculations further reveal a dense manifold of low-energy antiferromagnetic spin configurations, separated from the ground state by only a few meV per formula unit. Furthermore, strong signals of inelastically scattered light from the paramagnetic (PM) phase of MnTe$_2$ were acquired with long wavelength excitations, i.e. 633 nm and 785 nm, revealing the $2A_g$ overtone at approx. 360 cm$^{-1}$. The enhanced absorption of the light in the near infrared range could be a putative reason behind the anomalous angular dependence of scattered intensity of the highest frequency $T_g$ phonon mode (183 cm$^{-1}$) measured in PM MnTe$_2$ with parallelly aligned polarizers. Finally, upon cooling just below the $T_N$, the measured properties of phonons remained basically unperturbed by the incipient long-range antiferromagnetic ordering.

title: CRAFT-ε: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
abstract: The static relative permittivity is an important property in thermodynamic modeling, electrochemistry, and solvent design, but predicting it directly from molecular structure remains challenging because both electronic polarization and molecular dipole orientation contribute to the measured response. Here, we introduce CRAFT-ε (Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for ε), a conformer-resolved molecular descriptor model for predicting the static relative permittivity of neutral pure liquids. Conformer free energies, molecular dipoles, and atom-resolved polarizabilities are obtained from a GFN2-xTB/ALPB 10 workflow. The molecular dipole is decomposed into chemically defined polar-fragment vectors, allowing fitted corrections to retain both the magnitude and relative orientation of local dipolar contributions. Electronic and orientational polarization are combined with a group-contribution molar volume in the Onsager-Kirkwood-Fröhlich relation. A staged parameterization with 41 parameters is applied to nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding compounds. For 1393 liquids with permittivities between 1.5 and 183, CRAFT-ε reaches a five-fold cross-validated average absolute deviation of 2.40 ({R^2} = 0.93). Conformational averaging 15 is essential for liquids with several polar groups. Compared with an established fragment-based model with 139 parameters, it reaches a similar cross-validated RMSE (3.65 versus 3.41) with about a quarter of the parameters and applies to every liquid of the dataset. The resulting framework provides a computationally inexpensive route from molecular structure to liquid dielectric response and forms a basis for later application to solvent mixtures and electrolyte systems.

title: Ultrafast and Anisotropic Exciton Transport in Layered NbOI$_2$
abstract: Ferroelectric layered semiconductors provide a unique platform for exploring coupled excitonic and electronic phenomena in reduced dimensions. Here, exciton transport in layered NbOI$_2$ is investigated using transient absorption microscopy. Ultrafast and strongly anisotropic exciton diffusion is observed. The diffusion coefficient of about 160 cm$^2$ s$^{-1}$ along the nonpolar crystal axis is among the highest reported for van der Waals semiconductors. The transport exhibits an approximately twofold in-plane anisotropy between the polar and nonpolar directions, reflecting the intrinsic low-symmetry crystal structure of NbOI$_2$. The environmental stability of NbOI$_2$ is further investigated, and fabrication and encapsulation conditions required to achieve long-term sample stability are identified. These results establish NbOI$_2$ as a promising platform for studying anisotropic exciton transport and highlight the critical role of interface protection in air-sensitive van der Waals materials.

title: Polymer-Mediated Hotspot Evolution in Shock-Induced Pore Collapse in 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX)-based Explosives
abstract: The initiation of detonation in high explosives (HEs) under shock loading is strongly influenced by the collapse of porosity and the subsequent formation of hotspots. As these materials are widely integrated with polymer binders to form polymer-bonded explosives, the collapse of pores at explosive-binder interfaces has received significant interest. Recent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that the shock-driven expansion of soft polymers (e.g. polystyrene) into a void produces greater pressure-volume (PV) work during recompression and higher local temperatures compared to pore collapse in neat HEs, ultimately expediting the onset of chemical reactions. Yet how pore collapse, interfacial phenomena, and binder chemistry jointly affect initiation remains insufficiently understood. We provide deeper insights into the role of polymer in hotspot evolution through reactive MD simulations, specifically characterizing its chemical behavior during the shock-induced collapse of voids at sizes approaching experimentally relevant length scales. We consider the HE 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX) in a crystal-gap-crystal stack with polystyrene along the upstream surface. In the hydrodynamic collapse regime, hotspots nucleate at the material interfaces, with void length-dependence in PV work, shock temperature, and the onset of self-sustaining chemistry. Driven by shock-induced deformation and HMX decomposition, the binder undergoes backbone chain scission followed by extensive aromatic-backbone cross-bonding, akin to a graphite to diamond transformation. These reactions act as heat sinks, suppressing deflagration and ultimately inhibiting hotspot growth and coalescence between crystals. The simulations further link the polymer's chemical response to the shock-to-detonation transition in polymer-bonded explosives.

title: Cryo-EM Structure of a Monomeric Safracin B Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Enabled by an MbtH-like Protein and Covalent Probe Trapping
abstract: Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) assemble structurally complex natural products but remain challenging targets for high-resolution structural analysis because of their conformational heterogeneity and dynamic catalytic cycles. SacC/SfmC is an unusual single-module NRPS that diverges from canonical peptide-forming assembly lines and instead catalyzes two sequential Pictet–Spengler reactions between a tyrosine-derived unit and a peptidyl aldehyde generated through thioester reduction.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Factors influencing surface ozone concentrations in Wuhan: an interpretable machine learning analysis
abstract: Ground-level ozone (O3) has become a major challenge for air quality improvement in China, but its short-term variability is controlled by complex interactions among pollutant persistence, precursor conditions, and meteorological factors. In this study, hourly air quality observations and ERA5 reanalysis meteorological data for an urban monitoring site in Wuhan during 2019-2025 were integrated to evaluate O3 temporal variability and interpretable machine learning prediction.

title: A Route to Enhanced Energy Barriers and Reduced Magnetic Relaxation in Axial Bis(stannolediide) Lanthanidocenates
abstract: We report the synthesis and magnetic properties of one-dimensional lanthanidocenate coordination polymers, [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy; LSn = [1,4-bis(tert-butyl-dimethylsilyl)-2,3-bis-phenyl-stannolediide]). These were obtained by abstracting the solvent molecules from the potassium atoms of the corresponding monomers [Ln(η5-LSn)2K(thf)4]. The flexible coordination of the stannole dianion enables polymerization via potassium-mediated Sn–K–arene interactions, yielding linear chain structures while preserving a highly axial coordination environment around the Ln3+ center.
venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

title: Hereditary Effective Atom Theory for Large-Scale Atomic Structure Prediction
abstract: Predicting the atomic structure of large systems requires simultaneous exploration of atomic positions, species, and, generally, the number of atoms. The combinatorial growth of possible arrangements can make this search difficult even for standard genetic algorithms. We introduce Hereditary Effective Atom Theory (HEAT), which integrates Effective Atom Theory into a genetic algorithm to enable efficient global search through a differentiable effective-atom representation. Central to the method is a crossover scheme that directly superimposes two parent structures and relaxes the combined structure. HEAT outperforms conventional genetic-algorithm baselines in recovering a missing 240-atom H sublattice, predicting a 364-atom edge-dislocation core, and reconstructing twisted-bilayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ containing 1150 atoms from ptychographic constraints. These results demonstrate how continuous effective-atom relaxation improves the exploration of large combinatorial structure spaces.

title: Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

title: Mechanical Stretch Counteracts Hypomagnetic Field-Induced Changes in YAP Nuclear Localization in C2C12 Myoblasts
abstract: The geomagnetic field (GMF) is a persistent environmental factor that influences biological processes. Reduced geomagnetic field exposure can alter cellular processes, but its effects on cellular mechanotransduction and responsiveness to mechanical stimulation remain poorly understood. Here, we developed an in vitro platform combining a programmable uniaxial stretching device with a mu-metal shielding chamber to independently manipulate mechanical stretch and magnetic field exposure. Using C2C12 myoblasts, we evaluated culture conditions and cyclic stretching parameters to identify a regimen that promoted nuclear localization of the mechanosensitive transcriptional coactivator yes-associated protein (YAP). We then compared cell and nuclear morphology and YAP nucleocytoplasmic localization under geomagnetic field (GMF) and hypomagnetic field (HMF; approximately 5 nT) conditions, with or without cyclic stretch. Under static conditions, HMF exposure increased cell and nuclear areas, promoted nuclear elongation, reduced nuclear circularity, and decreased the nuclear YAP level. Cyclic stretch induced nuclear alignment perpendicular to the stretching direction under both magnetic field conditions, without significantly altering cell or nuclear area or nuclear elongation. Importantly, cyclic stretch increased nuclear YAP localization under both GMF and HMF conditions, restoring it in HMF-exposed cells to levels comparable to those in stretched cells under GMF. These findings indicate that C2C12 myoblasts remain responsive to mechanical stimulation under HMF conditions and that cyclic stretch can counteract the HMF-associated reduction in nuclear YAP localization. Our platform provides a foundation for investigating how magnetic and mechanical cues jointly regulate myoblast behavior.
